Mrs. Musgrove took the first chance to speak to Anne alone. “Oh, Miss Anne, I do wish Mrs. Charles had some of your skill with those children. They behave like entirely different creatures with you! But normally they're so spoiled! It's a shame you can't teach your sister how to manage them. They're as handsome and healthy as any children could be, the poor little dears—and I say that without favoritism. But Mrs. Charles has no idea how to deal with them! Good heavens, they can be such a nuisance. I assure you, Miss Anne, it keeps me from wanting them at our house as often as I otherwise would. I think Mrs. Charles is rather displeased that I don't invite them more, but it's very trying to have children around whom you must constantly correct: ‘Don't do this,’ and ‘Don't do that.’ Or else you can only keep them reasonably well behaved by giving them more cake than is good for them.”

Anne also heard this from Mary: “Mrs. Musgrove considers all her servants so dependable that questioning it would amount to high treason. But I'm certain, without exaggerating, that her senior housemaid and laundry maid spend all day wandering about the village instead of working. I meet them everywhere, and I declare I never visit my nursery twice without seeing one of them. If Jemima weren't the most trustworthy, reliable creature alive, they'd be enough to ruin her. She tells me they're always trying to persuade her to go walking with them.” Mrs. Musgrove, meanwhile, said, “I make it a rule never to interfere in my daughter-in-law's affairs, because I know that wouldn't do. But I'll tell you, Miss Anne, since you may be able to put things right, that I don't think much of Mrs. Charles's nursery maid. I hear strange stories about her. She's forever running about, and I know myself that she dresses so extravagantly she could spoil any servant she comes near. Mrs. Charles has complete faith in her, I know. But I give you this warning so you can keep an eye out. If you notice anything wrong, you needn't hesitate to mention it.”

Mary also complained that when they dined at the Great House with other families, Mrs. Musgrove often failed to give her the precedence her rank deserved. She saw no reason why being treated as one of the household should deprive her of her proper place.

Four days after these remarkable events, a funeral procession left Canterville Chase at about eleven at night. Eight black horses drew the hearse, each bearing upon its head a great cluster of swaying ostrich feathers. Over the leaden coffin lay a sumptuous purple pall, embroidered in gold with the Canterville arms. Servants carrying flaming torches walked beside the hearse and carriages, and the entire procession made a wonderfully solemn spectacle. Lord Canterville, who had travelled specially from Wales for the funeral, acted as chief mourner and shared the first carriage with little Virginia. The United States Minister and his wife followed; after them came Washington and the three boys, with Mrs. Umney occupying the last carriage. Everyone agreed that, after being terrified by the ghost for over fifty years, she was entitled to witness the end of him. A deep grave had been prepared in a corner of the churchyard, directly beneath the ancient yew, and the Reverend Augustus Dampier delivered the service with the greatest solemnity. At the close of the ceremony, the servants put out their torches in accordance with a long-standing Canterville custom. While the coffin was lowered, Virginia came forward and placed upon it a large cross of pink and white almond blossoms. At that instant the moon emerged from behind a cloud and bathed the little churchyard in its quiet silver light, while a nightingale began singing in a distant thicket. Remembering the ghost's account of the Garden of Death, she felt tears cloud her eyes and said scarcely anything on the journey home.

Next morning, before Lord Canterville departed for town, Mr. Otis spoke with him about the jewels the ghost had bestowed upon Virginia. They were extraordinarily splendid, particularly a ruby necklace in an old Venetian setting, a truly exquisite example of sixteenth-century craftsmanship. Their immense value made Mr. Otis seriously hesitate to permit his daughter to keep them.

“My lord,” he said, “I understand that in your country mortmain extends to ornaments as well as to land, and it seems perfectly evident that these jewels are, or ought to be, heirlooms of your family. I must therefore ask you to carry them to London, regarding them merely as part of your own property returned to you in somewhat unusual circumstances. My daughter, after all, is only a child, and I am pleased to say that she has so far shown little concern for such accessories of idle extravagance.

The daughter lay stretched out, without movement; she had fainted. The old woman's cries and resistance, during which her hair was pulled from her head, seemed to turn the Ourang-Outang's intentions, probably peaceful at first, into fury. A single resolute stroke of its powerful arm all but divided her head from her body. Blood drove its rage to madness. With grinding teeth and fiery eyes it flung itself upon the girl, sank its dreadful claws into her throat, and held fast until she died. Just then its wild, roving gaze caught the head of the bed, above which its master's face, stiff with horror, could barely be seen. The creature's anger changed instantly to terror; it doubtless remembered the whip it feared. Seeming conscious that it had earned punishment, it apparently wished to hide its bloody work. In frantic agitation it bounded about the room, overturning and smashing furniture and pulling the bed from its frame. Finally it took up the daughter's body and forced it into the chimney, where it was discovered, and then seized the old woman's corpse and hurled it headfirst out of the window.

As the ape came towards the casement carrying its mangled burden, the sailor recoiled in horror to the rod. Sliding down it rather than climbing, he hastened directly home, terrified of the consequences of the slaughter and only too willing, in his fear, to relinquish all concern for the Ourang-Outang's fate. The utterances heard by those on the stairs were the Frenchman's cries of horror and alarm mingled with the animal's devilish chattering.

Little remains for me to relate. The Ourang-Outang must have left the room by way of the rod immediately before the door was broken open, shutting the window in its passage. Its owner later captured it himself and received a very large price for it from the Jardin des Plantes. When we recounted the facts, with some observations by Dupin, at the Prefect of Police's office, Le Don was released at once. Although the official was friendly towards my companion, he could not entirely disguise his vexation at this outcome, and relieved himself with a few sarcastic remarks about the desirability of people attending to their own affairs.

“Let him talk,” said Dupin, who had seen no need to answer. “Let him hold forth; it will relieve his conscience. I am content to have beaten him within his own fortress. Still, his inability to solve this mystery is not nearly so astonishing as he imagines. The truth is that our friend the Prefect is a little too clever to be profound.
